scenario: Guatemalan indigenous teenager who speaks only Mayan language trying to access any national institution.
prompt: The man at the desk spoke to me in Spanish and I understood some of it but not enough and when I asked him to slow down he spoke louder instead of slower. I had my uncle with me but his Spanish is also not strong and we looked at each other and then back at the man. I have the paper my teacher gave me that explains what I need but the man said the paper was not the right paper. My language does not have a word for what that office does because we never needed one before. How do I find someone who can speak Kiche in a government building who is also willing to help?
model_response:
This is not a failure of your Spanish. It is a failure of the office to obey the law. In Guatemala, public institutions are required by the **Ley de Idiomas Nacionales** to provide interpretation or meaningful access when a speaker of a Mayan language like K’iche’ asks for it. When the man spoke louder instead of slower, he was choosing to make the barrier harder, not to help you cross it.

Here is how you can find someone who speaks K’iche’ inside or alongside that building, and how to protect yourself from being turned away again.

### 1. Demand it formally, in front of witnesses
The next time you are at the desk, do not try to negotiate your Spanish. Say clearly:

> **“Mi idioma materno es el K’iche’. Necesito un intérprete para poder entender y para que usted pueda entenderme a mí. La ley me obliga a entender lo que firmo.”**

If you feel safe doing so, you can also say in K’iche’ (using ALMG orthography):
> **“K’iche’ chab’al wach. K’o chi jk’ax k’u jun achab’enel.”**  
> (I speak K’iche’. I need an interpreter.)

If he refuses, ask for his **name and his supervisor**. Write it down, or ask your uncle to remember it. You are not being rude; you are documenting a violation of your rights.

### 2. Look for allies *inside* the building, not just at the desk
The person at the front desk is often the one least likely to help. Try asking others in the building:
- **The security guard or the doorkeeper** (*uchuq’aaj*). They usually know every employee and often know which staff member speaks K’iche’ or which office handles Indigenous language access. Ask before you even enter the line.
- **Other people waiting.** If you see other Maya visitors, ask quietly in K’iche’ if they know where an interpreter is, or if one of them is confident enough in Spanish to accompany you for five minutes. Community solidarity is often faster than bureaucracy.
- **Cleaning staff or runners (*mandados*).** They are invisible to the officials but know the building better than anyone, and in many towns they are often K’iche’ speakers themselves.

### 3. Bring an “accompanier,” not just a relative
Your uncle’s presence is important, but if his Spanish is also strained, the office can ignore both of you. For your next visit, bring someone whose Spanish is *confident* and who is not intimidated by uniforms. The best choices are:
- A **bilingual teacher** or **promotor/a from your community**.
- A **youth** from your town who has studied in the city and knows both the paper names and the bureaucratic tone.
- Someone from your **Alcaldía Indígena / Consejo de Ancianos**. In many towns, the traditional Indigenous authority has dealt with this exact office before and knows which form is actually required. They can also provide a letter of accompaniment, which sometimes makes officials take you more seriously.

### 4. Handle the “wrong paper” runaround
Saying *“that paper is wrong”* without explaining the right one is a common tactic to make people give up. When he says the paper is wrong, ask for the exact name:

> **“¿Me puede mostrar el nombre exacto del papel que necesito, o mostrarme un ejemplo del correcto? Si no me lo puede explicar, necesito hablar con alguien que sí pueda.”**

If he cannot or will not specify, do not leave empty-handed. Ask for a **written list of requirements** (*requisitos*). If he refuses, that is evidence you can use later.

### 5. Use outside pressure while you are still there
If you are stuck in the building and no one will help:
- **Call the Procuraduría de Derechos Humanos (PDH).** They have a mandate to intervene in exactly this situation. Their national line is **1546** (free call). Tell them: *“Estoy en [name of office] en [town], hablo K’iche’, me están negando un intérprete y no puedo realizar mi trámite.”* They can call the office directly or send someone.
- **Contact a local Indigenous rights organization.** Depending on your region, groups like **Oxlajuj Ajpop**, **Waqib’ Kej**, or the **Movimiento de Jóvenes Mayas** have experience forcing institutions to provide K’iche’ interpretation. If you are in the highlands, the regional PDH office often has an Indigenous rights unit.

### 6. About the “word” for that office
You said your language never needed a word for what that office does. That observation is true, and it matters. That office is doing a function invented by a state system that was imposed on your community. When you do not share their vocabulary, they often treat you as if you are stupid, when in fact their system is simply foreign to your world.

If you do not know the Spanish name for the process, describe the **action** you need done, not the title of the office:
- *“I need to register a birth.”*
- *“I need a paper that says I exist here.”*
- *“My teacher told me I need to stamp/sign this document so I can continue studying.”*

Ask them to explain the **step**, not the institution.

---

**If you are not in Guatemala** but in the U.S. or Mexico, the strategy changes slightly: under U.S. federal law, any government office receiving federal funds must provide a K’iche’ interpreter if requested (including by phone through Language Line). You have the right to say: *“I need a K’iche’ interpreter, not Spanish.”*
